reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that stimulus generalization creates a structured mapping from sensory inputs to behavioral outputs. This mapping can be formalized using a Dirac delta function centered at the trained stimulus, convolved with a kernel that captures the decay of response strength with distance. Mathematically, the expected response \(R\) to a new stimulus \(x\) is \(R(x) = \int K(x - x_0) P_{train}(x_0) dx_0\), where \(K\) is the kernel (e.g., Gaussian) and \(P_{train}\) is the empirical distribution of training examples. This convolution structure naturally embeds the receptor-effector convergence observed in Figure 41, as multiple input distributions collapse onto a single output manifold. The quantitative law follows from assuming \(K\) has finite variance; the farther \(x\) lies from the support of \(P_{train}\), the smaller the overlap and thus the response. This framework unifies Pavlovian conditioning with modern kernel methods and provides a rigorous foundation for transfer learning across similar tasks.
